en: The line that Allah wrote
Is thus: let me face it.
Six times the telescope
Let me hold steady and extend.
If my bay horse does not come in all six,
If God will not grant it,
For six calves and forty yearlings
I bought Aktinte.
Let me draw it from its sheath,
Plunge it beneath my lower ribs,
Let me cut myself open.
Before I die at my son's hands,
Let me die by my own!
If he does not come in six looks,
If my wish is not granted,
Let me see the face of the next world.
On the day that takes me, let me shed my blood.
Six times through the telescope,
Without impatience, I, the passionate woman,
Let me look with care.
If he does not come in six looks,
If my wish is not granted,
After that let me die.'
Then your mother, built like a warrior,
Turned Akborchuk's head.
Sobbing as she offered prayer,
To God whose command is mighty
She cried out in repentance.
Turning its wheel,
The telescope left by Manas
She put right to her eye.
Turning its screw,
Bursting into tears,
She turned her swift steed's head.
That spirited woman, built like a warrior,
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykei
Stood looking through the telescope.
That unfortunate woman was bewildered,
Despairing of her borrowed life,
Unable to regain her composure,
Burning with terrible grief.
The slope of It-Torpu
Your sister-in-law caught sight of,
And at the sight she rejoiced greatly.
'For this grief-stricken head,
There must be a day when the Night of Power comes.
For this grieving, wretched head,
Today must be the day to see my only child!
God will grant my wish,
O Almighty, Bahauddin,
Today my Taitoru will come forward, will he not?!
For this head that never saw the sun,
There will be a time of sunshine.
For this head without fortune,
The dawn will break clear, will it not?!'
'God will quench my fire,
God will brighten my brow.
He will bind the hair at my nape,
My dear Taitoru,
Will wash away my widow's name, will he not?'
Crying out for joy,
Bursting into tears,
When she looked through the telescope,
Upon the ridge of It-Torpu,
Along Kezen-Kyr,
'When I count, Taitoru,
My swift steed is coming,
Behind sixty horses.
He has lowered his head to the ground,
My dear swift steed,
Has taken strides like a wild sheep.
He has lowered his neck to the ground,
Has taken immeasurable strides.
The wind cannot match his trot;
He has begun to run in full strength.
No beast can match his pace;
He has begun to run as never before.
When he slopes down the descent,
My dear swift steed,
His forelegs strike like a roe deer's.
When he pulls uphill,
His mane and tail spread wide.
When he reaches level plain,
His hooves drum upon the ground.
The black steel bit
Cracks in the creature's throat.
His maw opens wide,
White foam mixed with blood
Splashes upon his breast.
The black steel bit
Clatters against his throat.
His tail like strands of silk
Lashes against his flanks.'
Thus running, leaning forward,
His noble head like a deer's
Was wrapped in pitch-black dust.
'There is a night like the Night of Power;
There is a day to brighten my brow!
God will lift my sorrow,
Will still my grieving voice!
All my sorrow scattering,
My brow opening into brightness,
Among horses, the blaze-faced wondrous steeds—
Almambet and Chubak, their names paired—
Will surely turn their gaze toward me.
The heroes gone to the next world
Will come to aid the widow!
Upon a poor soul like me
The Almighty will turn his gaze.
The forty chiltens, Khydyr and Ilyas,
If they will it, the bay horse
They will all urge forward together!'
Saying these words then,
Your courageous sister-in-law Kanykei
Her dear currant-black eyes
Turned and wiped once more.
Crying out, 'Bahauddin,'
Sobbing, calling on the one God,
The king's great telescope
She took deftly in her hand,
Then put it to her eye.
Your sister-in-law looked again
And learned the horses' news.
At the spur of the yellow hills,
At the jutting mountain's headland,
Upon the ridge of Koruuchu,
Along the dark plain,
Taitoru was coming.
When she looked carefully through the telescope,
He was behind thirty wondrous steeds.
'Oh, my dear swift steed,
You were a renowned racehorse.
I tell my anguish to God!
Dear creature, you had sixty years of maturity.
Do not let my words grow cold.
Do not make them call me a crazed woman
And bring disgrace upon me.
Do not make me wail any longer,
O one Almighty Creator,
Do not make my eyes weep.
Do not make my words come to nothing,
Do not shame me.'
Protesting as she said this,
Upon the saddle-shaped ridge,
Your luckless sister-in-law,
Unable to stand grieving and weeping,
Wishing to die yet unable to die,
Unable to cut short her surviving life,
Her thoughts painfully divided,
As though stricken with wasting sickness,
The tears streamed from your mother's eyes.
Her poor heart would not grow still,
Was torn apart so many times.
The poor soul stood lamenting
On the plain where no crow flew.
Her grief and fear were
Of the child born from her womb,
Of her spring feeding a valley river.
The poor soul feared especially
That orphan born of herself.
Once more your unfortunate sister-in-law,
The poor woman built like a warrior,
Now gathered her senses.
Turning back, struggling,
Imploring the one God,
She looked through the telescope again.
Again observing her bay horse,
Again she learned his condition.
At the mist-covered spur,
At the headland of the gray hills,
Upon the ridge of Kezenche,
Taitoru was coming
Along broad Ak-Chiy.
'Again my swift steed is coming.'
He was behind twelve wondrous steeds then.
Her heart was torn apart,
Unable to stand and watch,
The tears streamed from your mother's eyes.
With golden forelock and tasseled belt,
Azyz Khan's only son,
The swift steed Taitoru,
Upon the bright horse Sarala,
Your Alake seemed to be driving forward.
Wearing yellow leather trousers,
Bearing a spear without a tassel,
A bare sword fastened at his side,
His sturdy waist girded,
When he saw seventy thousand troops,
He swept in and attacked,
Not a hair recoiling from death,
Never drawing back from dying.
Your champion with a guardian's support,
My champion, the son of light,
Had received a letter from Khan Kozho,
Had received the caliph's blessing.
That dear lion, born surpassing others,
Was also named the mighty conquering champion.
His amassed wealth was left in Kakan;
What he most desired was religion and faith.
His amassed wealth was left in Beijing;
What he cherished was faith.
The religions he chose and knew,
The caliph and sultan spiritual guides,
The religions he esteemed and knew,
The sultan spiritual guides in Mecca—
The true religion entered his dream,
Purity entered his heart.
Because of the Last Judgment,
Because that damned Hell exists,
Because of the next world,
Because a tormenting Hell exists,
He was cleansed of the dark religion,
Fled the unbelievers and became a stranger,
Scattered the wealth he had amassed,
Desired only faith.
Shrouding himself in the dark day,
His father the khan, Azyz Khan,
He implored, 'Become a Muslim.'
When his appeals would not bring him to the faith,
When he would not heed his words,
He cast away his golden throne.
His father Azyz Khan
He killed in Great Beijing.
He bloodied his silver throne,
Killed his father Kun Zhang-Zhung.
The holy man seen in his sleep,
Paradise and Hell seen in his dream—
For this wretched life of suffering,
He witnessed a most wondrous thing.
Surviving because he had not died,
When he had newly become a Muslim,
He took the warrior Mazhik along,
Made Altynai his companion.
His good days gone, he was oppressed.
From the forty thieving Chinese unbelievers,
The steel spear in his hand
He held and thrust without wavering.
With cotton belt and broad boots,
The monks' khan Konurbai
Fought him without pause for six months.
'That great idol made of bronze,
Calling it God,
How can I stand muttering before it?
From turbulent Hell
I shall free my soul,' he said.
'The faith I cherish is pure;
I shall reach Mecca and settle there,' he said.
'That great idol made of bronze,
Calling it God,' he said,
"How could I be an unbeliever?" he said.
He fought fiercely for six months;
He was struck from the flank.
His mother Altynay,
His forty companions and their wealth—
He lost them to China as spoils.
